sourceNotes: Seeded from RMS roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: RMS event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Margin dollars a department earns divided by the square footage it occupies, so a category producing $80,000 of margin on 400 feet returns $200 a foot and outranks one producing $120,000 on 900 feet.
terms.whyItMatters: A floor-plan roleplay that asks which department surrenders space to a new fixture is settled on margin per foot; the bigger seller frequently returns less per foot than the smaller one.

terms.definition: Margin dollars divided by the payroll hours a department consumed to produce them; a service-heavy category can beat a self-select one on margin percent and still lose on this figure once its selling hours are counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about trimming scheduled hours in one department turn on it — the judge wants the payroll dollar set against the margin it generated, not against sales volume.

terms.definition: Net sales divided by the running feet of fixture a category occupies, measured horizontally along the wall or gondola no matter how many shelves are stacked within it — the figure that decides how much of a four-foot section a slow SKU keeps.
terms.whyItMatters: Shelf-reset roleplays require justifying the transfer of a foot of space from one brand to another; linear productivity is the number that makes that defensible instead of arbitrary.

terms.definition: On-hand units divided by average weekly unit sales — 240 units moving 30 a week is eight weeks — converting a raw count into a forward statement about whether the store runs out before the next delivery or is still holding goods at markdown time.
terms.whyItMatters: In a replenishment roleplay the competitor must turn 'we have plenty' into a provable number the judge can check against the delivery cycle.

terms.definition: A reduction measured against the ticket the item carries today rather than its original price: a $50 item already cut to $40 and now moved to $30 is 25% off retail but 40% off original, and only the first figure may go on the sign.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-change roleplays and markdown math items both hinge on which base was used; quoting the off-original figure on a second reduction overstates the discount to the customer.

terms.definition: The upward price change that returns a temporarily reduced item toward its former ticket when a sale ends; it can offset the earlier reduction but never exceed it, because anything above the original price is an additional markup instead.
terms.whyItMatters: Weekend-promotion roleplays require showing that Monday's price restoration is a cancellation, not a markup — only cancellations net against the season's markdown dollars.

terms.definition: Everything that lowers the retail value of stock other than a full-price sale — markdowns, employee and customer discounts, and shrinkage — totalled and stated against net sales: $40,000 plus $6,000 plus $4,000 on $250,000 of sales is 20%.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which of four listed items belongs in the total, and roleplays ask a manager to explain why planned sales alone understate what the season's inventory must cover.

terms.definition: The gap between what the perpetual records say should be on hand and what the count actually finds, stated in retail dollars and as a percent of sales — books of $412,000 against a counted $398,600 on $1.2M of sales is a 1.1% loss.
terms.whyItMatters: The figure a loss-prevention roleplay opens with; the competitor has to separate genuine loss from paperwork causes such as uncounted transfers or unposted vendor returns before proposing a remedy.

terms.definition: An estimated loss booked each month between physical counts — usually last year's audited rate applied to current sales — so the P&L carries a steady charge, with a true-up entry correcting the estimate once the count lands.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why a store's monthly margin looks level and then drops sharply in the count month; a competitor asked why gross margin fell in one period must name the true-up rather than blame pricing.

terms.definition: The share of counted locations whose on-hand matched the system within tolerance, scored per location rather than per unit — 47 of 50 bins clean is 94%, and a bin wrong by a single unit fails outright.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay that sets up a counting program has to state the standard (commonly 95%+ on A items) and the tolerance; 'we count often' is not a measurable answer for a judge.

terms.definition: The percentage of tagged units a handheld or overhead reader actually detects in one pass; retail programs hold it near 95-99%, and every point below that inflates apparent loss because an unread tag looks exactly like a missing unit.
terms.whyItMatters: In an inventory-accuracy roleplay the competitor must explain why a tag-based count still needs a stated standard — a 92% read on 10,000 units invents 800 losses that were never stolen.

terms.definition: The share of audited facings matching the plan in position, facing count and signing, scored per section — a four-foot bay carrying 40 facings with 6 wrong scores 85%, not 'mostly right'.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-funded resets and display allowances are paid against an audited percentage, so a roleplay about losing that funding turns on producing the number rather than describing the effort.

terms.definition: How many units sit behind the front unit of one shelf position — depth times stack height — which caps what can sell between deliveries: 9 units per position on a shelf served twice a week limits that SKU to 18 units a week regardless of demand.
terms.whyItMatters: The arithmetic behind 'add a facing': a competitor asking for more space must show current capacity falls short of the sell rate, not merely that the shelf looked empty at closing.

terms.definition: Shelf capacity for one position divided by average daily unit sales — 12 units against 4 a day is three days — telling the store whether a SKU survives a weekend without a mid-day fill from the backroom.
terms.whyItMatters: Space-allocation roleplays expect any item scoring below the delivery interval to earn another facing or a service visit, and the judge wants that comparison stated out loud.

terms.definition: Sales per square foot earned in a promotional end-of-aisle position divided by the same figure for the store's in-line shelving; a display running under roughly 3x in-line productivity is not earning the premium space it sits in.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect a promotional plan to defend which product wins the endcap with a ratio, not with an opinion about which brand deserves the exposure this month.

terms.definition: A category's percentage of linear feet compared against its percentage of store sales, read as the ratio of the two — 12% of the space driving 8% of sales indexes 0.67 and is over-spaced no matter how large its absolute sales look.
terms.whyItMatters: The single number that turns a floor-plan roleplay into an argument: it names which categories give feet up and which take them, and it survives a judge's follow-up question.

terms.definition: Pick labor, packaging and outbound parcel freight charged against one order line filled from a store's selling stock — normally several dollars above a distribution-center pick, so the markdown avoided on aged inventory has to exceed it before the routing pays.
terms.whyItMatters: An omnichannel roleplay asking whether a store should accept online orders is answered by setting this cost against the markdown avoided, not by calling the service convenient.

terms.definition: The share of pickup customers who buy something additional at the counter — attached transactions divided by pickups, so 300 pickups yielding 66 add-on sales is 22% — and the figure that makes an otherwise unprofitable online order pay.
terms.whyItMatters: Justifying pickup-desk staffing in a roleplay requires converting those add-on sales into dollars per pickup and comparing them with the labor hours the desk consumes.

terms.definition: Correctly filled order lines as a percent of lines picked, scored per line rather than per order — a five-line order with one wrong item is 80% — and store-fulfilment programs generally hold it at 98% or better.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about online-order complaints needs the error quantified per line before a fix such as scan-verify at packing can be justified to the judge on cost grounds.

terms.definition: Whether a customer standing in the aisle can actually pick the product up, measured at the shelf instead of in the system — a store can show 99% in stock on the books and still be empty at the point of sale because the units sit in the backroom.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward the competitor who separates what the inventory report claims from what the shelf shows when asked why sales fell on an item that never registered as out of stock.

terms.definition: Employee theft committed through the register — passing merchandise to a friend without scanning it, or applying a discount the customer is not entitled to — which surfaces as shrink but leaves a transaction trail the register data can be mined for.
terms.whyItMatters: Loss-prevention roleplays ask how internal loss differs from shoplifting and what evidence supports discipline; this is the case exception reporting exists to catch.

terms.definition: Mining point-of-sale data for the transactions that break a pattern — no-sales, voids, receiptless refunds, discounts clustered on one cashier — and flagging only those for review instead of auditing every sale.
terms.whyItMatters: The expected answer when a judge asks how a store investigates internal loss without watching every cashier; naming the specific exception types is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Accepting at a store counter the return of an item purchased on the website, which puts the unit back into that location's sellable stock and its markdown exposure even though the store never booked the original sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about managers resisting online returns turn on this split: the store absorbs the labor and the inventory risk while the online channel keeps the revenue credit.

terms.definition: Shoppers who buy divided by the door-counter traffic that walked in — the middle term of sales = traffic x rate x average sale — so moving 18% to 19% on 4,000 weekly visitors spending $38 adds $1,520 a week without one additional shopper.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking a store manager to defend added weekend hours is won by pricing the conversion point those hours buy against what they cost, rather than promising better service.

terms.definition: Physical units sold divided by transactions rung — a three-pack scanned once still counts three, which is where it parts company with items per ticket — and sales are transactions x this figure x average unit retail, so 0.2 more units across 900 tickets at $12 is $2,160.
terms.whyItMatters: Suggestive-selling roleplays are scored on converting 'sell more add-ons' into the exact per-ticket unit lift the store's sales goal requires, then naming the coaching that produces it.

terms.definition: Units projected to be left over when a season closes — on hand minus weeks remaining times the current rate, so 400 pieces with six weeks to go selling 30 a week strand 220 — and that leftover, not the calendar, sets how deep the first reduction has to be while selling weeks still exist.
terms.whyItMatters: A markdown roleplay hinges on proving the cut is needed now; the judge wants the leftover projection, not an assurance that the item might still sell through.

terms.definition: A fixed schedule of reductions an aged item steps through — 25% at week eight, 40% at twelve, 60% at sixteen — where each step is sized to multiply the sell rate enough to clear the units still on hand before the next step lands, not merely to look cheaper than last week.
terms.whyItMatters: Clearance roleplays ask why an item was cut on that date at that depth; naming the step, the week and the units it must move is the answer that scores, and 'it wasn't moving' is not.

terms.definition: The share of a random shelf sample that rings at the posted price, audited by weights-and-measures inspectors on 50 items against a 98% floor — two misses fail the lot — with overcharges scored on their own so undercharges can never net them out.
terms.whyItMatters: An inspection roleplay turns on the sample size, the pass mark and that asymmetry; 'we correct wrong prices quickly' does not survive the judge's first follow-up question.

terms.definition: A positive on-hand the shelf cannot actually produce, which costs more than plain loss because automatic replenishment only fires below the reorder point: a stuck count of four against a point of three orders nothing ever again, so stores hunt it with a stock-on-hand-but-zero-sales rule instead of waiting for the annual count.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a top seller quietly stopped selling while never once recording an out-of-stock, the competitor has to name the record error that froze ordering and the audit trigger that surfaces it.

terms.definition: Store labor dollars measured against net sales, of which only a part can actually move: a site running 8% on $60,000 spends $4,800, and if $1,900 covers management and open-to-close coverage, a 10% sales miss has to come out of the $2,900 that flexes — about a fifth of those hours.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand a manager a sales shortfall and a payroll target are scored on cutting from the flexible pool with the arithmetic shown, not on trimming every department equally.

terms.definition: Growth measured only across locations open through both periods — customarily thirteen months, with remodels and relocations pulled out of the base — which is how a chain opening doors posts record total revenue while this figure falls and the existing fleet is in fact shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks whether the company is really growing, the expected answer defines the base first and then explains what the total-sales headline was concealing.

terms.definition: How much of a building's footprint actually holds sellable fixtures — 16,800 feet of 24,000 is 70% — and the reason two stores' productivity numbers cannot be compared until both use the same base, since rent is charged on every gross foot while sales come only from the selling ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Benchmarking roleplays fall apart when one store divides sales by gross feet and its comparison divides by selling feet; the competitor has to state the base before quoting the figure.

terms.definition: Online order lines a store accepts and then cannot locate, divided by lines routed to it — each one forfeits the sale plus the pick labor already spent — and the remedy is arithmetic rather than effort: lifting the routing buffer so any SKU at two or fewer on hand is never offered online removes most of them.
terms.whyItMatters: An omnichannel roleplay about cancellation emails is answered by weighing that buffer against the sellable demand it hides, which is the trade-off the judge is waiting to hear.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Averages the size of forecast misses ignoring their direction — the sum of |actual − forecast| ÷ the number of periods — which keeps the error in the product's own units instead of percentages, and roughly 1.25 times this figure approximates one standard deviation of forecast error for setting a buffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-error items hand six periods of actuals and forecasts and expect this average computed; it is also the denominator of the tracking signal, so an error here quietly breaks the control check built on top of it.

terms.definition: Moore's gap between the 13.5% early-adopter band, which buys on the promise of a breakthrough and tolerates an incomplete product, and the 34% early majority, which buys only on references from people already like themselves; products stall in it because the two groups will not act as references for each other, and the standard bridge is dominating one narrow beachhead segment until its references become credible to the next group.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay shows strong early sales that suddenly flatten, naming this gap and the beachhead fix is the diagnosis a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The price a manufacturer recommends retailers charge for a product.
terms.whyItMatters: MSRP frames legal and ethical pricing and channel relationships.

terms.definition: Measures how closely the lines relate in production, distribution, and end use -- something neither width nor depth can show: two firms each carrying 4 lines and 40 items differ sharply when one sells only refrigerated foods through grocers and the other sells food, tires, and insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification questions ask whether a proposed line fits; the scoring point is that the new line shares plants or channels with the existing ones, not that it sounds related.

terms.definition: A legal entity separate from its owners that can own property, contract, and be sued.
terms.whyItMatters: Incorporation shields owners from personal liability for business debts.

terms.definition: An ad's key elements — headline, copy, visuals, call to action, and branding.
terms.whyItMatters: Each component ensures the ad communicates its message persuasively.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Recommending additional products based on the customer's current purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Suggestive selling raises transaction value and meets more needs.

terms.definition: Swapping direct identifiers for tokens while keeping the re-identification key stored separately, which leaves the file still legally personal data under GDPR Article 4(5) and still inside the regulation's reach; true anonymization destroys that key irreversibly, and only then does the data fall out of scope entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics-in-data-mining item asks whether replacing customer names with ID numbers lets a firm share the file freely, and the graded answer is that it does not while the key survives.

terms.term: Hazard analysis and critical control points
terms.definition: A seven-principle food-safety system that analyzes biological, chemical and physical hazards, fixes the specific steps where a hazard can be eliminated or controlled, sets a measurable critical limit at each such step, then monitors, corrects, verifies and records — control at those points, not final-product testing, is what proves safety.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about food handling reward naming the control step and its measurable limit — a cooking temperature or a holding time — instead of general cleanliness advice.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of whether people define themselves as 'I' or as part of a permanent in-group: the United States scores about 91, the highest of the fifty-plus countries surveyed, and Guatemala about 6. It answers a different question than power distance, which measures tolerance of unequal authority, and a country can be strongly collectivist while low in power distance. The communication consequence differs accordingly - a high score licenses naming one person's contribution and negotiating one-to-one, a low score requires the group to settle a position before any single voice states it.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why singling out one employee for praise backfired with an overseas team is scored on this dimension, not on generic 'cultural differences.'

terms.definition: Rates an object in the space between two opposite adjectives, modern against old-fashioned or cheap against expensive, usually across seven positions, and the item means plotted in sequence form a brand profile that can be overlaid on a competitor's; a Likert item by contrast measures agreement with one written statement.
terms.whyItMatters: Image and positioning studies are reported as these profiles, so a competitor asked how to measure how a brand is perceived versus a rival names this instrument.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: (actual minus planned) / planned x 100, carried on every line of the marketing plan: $92,000 delivered against a $100,000 forecast is -8%. The sign alone does not say good or bad — negative on revenue is unfavorable, negative on expense is favorable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-year review items give planned and actual columns and ask which lines need action; competitors who read every negative as a problem flag the underspent line that is actually helping.

terms.definition: The number-two or number-three firm by share — roughly 30% against a leader's 40% in Kotler's benchmark structure, above a follower's 20% and a nicher's 10% — which attacks the leader or smaller rivals head-on rather than imitating; a firm with the same share that deliberately copies the leader and avoids provoking retaliation is a follower, so the label is set by chosen posture, not by size alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Strategy roleplays that hand you a share table expect the four positions named and the posture defended; calling every non-leader a competitor loses the distinction.

terms.definition: Infers elasticity from the direction revenue moves after a price change: if raising price raises total revenue, demand is inelastic; if revenue falls, demand is elastic; if revenue holds steady, elasticity is unitary. It needs no coefficient at all, unlike the midpoint calculation it substitutes for.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges accept this shortcut when a candidate has to justify a price increase on the spot without the data to compute an elasticity coefficient.

terms.definition: Letting one strong impression, often a single outstanding trait, lift every unrelated rating for the same person; its inverse, the horns effect, drags them all down from one bad impression. In an appraisal it shows up as suspiciously uniform scores across dimensions that ought to vary, and the standard counter is rating every employee on one dimension at a time before moving to the next.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows an evaluation form with identical scores in every category is testing this, and an HR roleplay on fixing a review process is scored on the dimension-by-dimension fix.

terms.definition: A purchase for which buyers accept no substitute and will pass closer outlets to reach one brand -- insistence, not preference; a shopping good is one buyers compare on price, quality, and style across several stores and will happily switch brands on to save money.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution questions follow from this classification: specialty goods justify exclusive distribution and few outlets, while shopping goods need enough outlets for comparison to happen.

terms.definition: An auction in which the winner pays one increment above the runner-up's bid rather than the amount they themselves bid, so a $4.00 bid beating a $2.50 bid clears at $2.51 — which is why bidding true value can never cost more than that value is worth.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-buying items ask why an advertiser should enter its real maximum instead of shading the bid down; the mechanic, not the strategy, is the answer, and competitors who guess pay-what-you-bid get it backwards.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: Exaggerated subjective praise no reasonable buyer would treat as fact — the finest coffee in town — which creates no liability, as opposed to a misrepresentation, a specific factual claim about performance, condition or origin that does. The dividing test is whether the statement could be proven false.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethical selling roleplays plant a tempting overstatement, and knowing that this machine will cut your costs in half is a checkable claim while our machines are the best is not keeps you on the right side of the rubric.

terms.definition: The European rule granting individuals rights of access, correction, portability and erasure over their own data, requiring a documented lawful basis before any processing begins, forcing breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours, and capping fines at the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: An international e-commerce roleplay asks what changes when the site starts shipping to Ireland, and the answer is these specific obligations and their clock, not a general promise of privacy.

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share, the number of dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit — a rough gauge of how much growth is priced in.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a client on whether a stock looks expensive in an investing roleplay turns on this multiple, not on the share price alone.

terms.definition: A company-wide philosophy making every employee responsible for continuous improvement and customer-defined quality; quality assurance is the narrower set of process activities designed to prevent defects, and quality control is the narrowest — the inspection and testing that finds defects after production.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items line up the three terms and ask which one an inspection station belongs to; sorting philosophy from prevention from detection is the whole question.

terms.definition: Whatever shape the population takes, the distribution of sample means approaches a normal curve as the sample grows, with n of at least 30 used as the working threshold; that is the reason a margin of error can be computed from a single sample even when the underlying spending data is heavily skewed by a few large buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the justification a judge wants when a research plan projects one sample's average onto the whole market, and it is why a 12-person sample cannot carry that projection.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Divides the running cumulative forecast error by the mean absolute deviation to test whether misses are random noise or one-sided drift; a value wandering past ±4 says the model is systematically off and must be re-fit rather than nudged, while a value oscillating around zero says the error is noise and the model should be left alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-control questions supply a cumulative error and a MAD and want both the ratio and the keep-or-refit call against the limit, not a general remark that the forecast looks wrong.

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: Calendar days from the day a requisition is approved to the day a candidate accepts the offer, averaged across openings. Its near-twin, time to hire, starts the clock later — at the day the hired person first applied — so time to fill measures the whole requisition including sourcing delay while time to hire measures only the candidate's own journey, and a 62-day time to fill can sit on top of a 19-day time to hire.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you both numbers and ask which one proves the bottleneck is job-posting approval rather than the interview loop.

terms.definition: Advertising a product at an attractive price with no real intent to sell it, then disparaging it or claiming it is unavailable to move the shopper onto a costlier item. The FTC treats this as a deceptive practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act; a loss leader differs because the advertiser genuinely stocks and sells the promoted item at the promoted price.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics items put a candidate on a sales floor where the advertised model is sold out every single week, and the judge wants the practice named and refused.

terms.definition: Moves a new product through fixed stages separated by go/kill reviews with written criteria, so a project can die at any gate -- screening, business analysis, development, testing, launch; the long-standing planning ratio is roughly 7 serious ideas entering for every 1 commercial success.
terms.whyItMatters: Development roleplays ask what happens between an idea and a launch; the scoring point is that each gate can kill the project, not that the stages happen in order.

terms.definition: Coordinating all promotion for one consistent message across channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across touchpoints reinforces the message and maximizes impact.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: A seller's factual affirmation, description, sample or model that becomes part of the basis of the bargain, created by the statement itself with no formal words and no intent required — where an implied warranty arises automatically from the sale by operation of law. A rep quoting a performance figure in a presentation can create one without meaning to.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling exam items ask which of four salesperson statements creates a binding promise, and the answer is always the specific, checkable one rather than the general praise beside it.

terms.definition: Planning credential CFP Board grants to a candidate who holds a bachelor's degree, completes registered coursework, passes a 170-question exam given in two three-hour sessions, and logs 6,000 hours of professional experience — or 4,000 hours under a supervised apprenticeship — then renews with 30 continuing-education hours every two years, 2 of them CFP Board ethics. Against a licence that only obliges a recommendation to be suitable, the difference is the standard of care: the holder must act as a fiduciary and place the client's interest ahead of their own whenever advice is given.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance roleplays that make a competitor explain designations to a client reward the fiduciary-versus-suitability line, and exam items on ongoing education use the 30-hour, two-year renewal as the tested number.

terms.definition: Standards governing the responsible collection, use, protection, and sharing of information.
terms.whyItMatters: Privacy and data-governance dilemmas are common in modern business scenarios.

terms.definition: An energy-control procedure requiring every power source to a machine to be isolated, physically locked, and tagged by the individual servicing it — with the rule that only that person may remove their own lock — so no one can restart equipment while a colleague is inside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment-safety roleplays about a maintenance injury expect this named procedure and the one-worker-one-lock rule, not general advice to turn the machine off.

terms.definition: Compares the counts actually observed in a cross-tabulation against the counts expected if the two variables were unrelated, summing (observed minus expected) squared divided by expected across every cell, with degrees of freedom of (rows minus 1) times (columns minus 1). It works on category counts, where a test of means cannot be run at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A cross-tab of purchase versus age bracket looks different by eye long before the difference is real, and this is the test that decides whether the pattern survives sampling noise.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: Scores every step of a forecasting process by the accuracy points it adds over the naive baseline — baseline MAPE 20%, statistical model 17%, sales-team override 19% — so the model step is worth +3 points and the override is worth −2 and should be removed from the process rather than coached.
terms.whyItMatters: Process-improvement items ask which forecasting step to cut, and the negative-value step is the answer; it is also the numeric way a plan review argues that field overrides are hurting the number instead of helping it.

terms.definition: A sequenced change program running from establishing urgency, building a guiding coalition, forming a vision, and communicating it, through empowering action, generating short-term wins, consolidating gains, and anchoring the change in culture; it is a longer prescription than Lewin's three-stage unfreeze-change-refreeze cycle.
terms.whyItMatters: Management written events about rolling out a new system are graded on the early urgency and coalition steps, which is where most stalled rollouts are diagnosed.

terms.definition: A brand's own market share divided by the share of its single largest competitor — 20% against a leader's 40% is 0.5x, and only the market leader can score above 1.0 — which is the horizontal axis of the growth-share matrix; two brands holding an identical absolute share therefore land in opposite quadrants depending on how dominant the rival directly above each of them happens to be.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that reports 20% share and calls it strong is answered by asking what the leader holds; the ratio, not the raw percentage, is what drives the portfolio decision.

terms.definition: Removes the direction bias in an elasticity calculation by dividing each change by the average of the two values: (change in Q / [(Q1+Q2)/2]) divided by (change in P / [(P1+P2)/2]). A plain percentage change gives one answer for a price rise and a different one for the identical fall; this gives the same coefficient both ways.
terms.whyItMatters: Elasticity math on the finance exam is scored against this formula, so a competitor using simple percentage change lands on a distractor answer.

terms.definition: Portable, shorter-lived business goods bought routinely by middle managers and written off over a few years -- hand tools, laptops, forklifts; an installation is the major capital asset such as a plant or a production line, approved by top management on a multi-year capital budget.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business selling roleplays are scored on calling on the right buyer: the pair differs by who signs, so pitching an installation to a department manager is a scoring miss.

terms.definition: The Media Rating Council standard that counts a display impression only when at least 50% of its pixels hold the screen for one continuous second — two continuous seconds for video — so a campaign can serve 1,000,000 impressions and have only 600,000 of them count.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay where the client is billed for impressions the audience never had a chance to see is resolved by this standard, and exam items use the gap between served and counted impressions to test whether the competitor knows the threshold.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: One member's ability to make another do what it otherwise would not, drawn from the five French-and-Raven bases: coercive (threatening to cut supply or shelf space), reward (extra margin or funds), expert (knowledge the other lacks), referent (the partner wants the association), and legitimate (a contract already requires it). Coercive power gets compliance but raises conflict; referent and expert power get cooperation.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-relationship roleplay asks how you would move a resistant distributor; naming the base you are using, and why coercion would cost you the relationship, is the scored discrimination.

terms.definition: Developing a base of regular customers who return to buy again.
terms.whyItMatters: A strong clientele provides stable revenue and drives growth.

terms.definition: Copies only the blocks changed since the previous backup of any type, so each nightly run is the smallest possible, but restoring requires the last full backup plus every one of these runs applied in order since it — and a single missing or corrupt link breaks the entire chain behind it.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-storage items ask why a company whose nightly job finishes in four minutes still needed nine hours to recover, and the restore chain is the reason.

terms.definition: Outsourcing physical distribution functions — warehousing, transportation, freight handling — to a provider that owns trucks and buildings; a fourth-party provider owns no assets and instead manages the other providers, acting as a single coordinating layer over several third parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution-strategy questions ask which outsourcing level fits a firm that lacks not trucks but the ability to coordinate several carriers, and the asset-owning versus orchestrating split is the answer.

terms.definition: Shows respondents whole product profiles whose attributes are deliberately traded off against one another, say three price points crossed with three warranty lengths and two brands, then derives a part-worth utility for every level from the choices made, revealing what a feature is worth in dollars; asking directly how important price is can never produce that trade-off.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing a feature bundle for a client, this is the method that answers how much a second-year warranty is worth, and importance ratings simply cannot.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Holds every commercial seller in the distribution chain answerable for a product defective in manufacture, design, or warning that reached the user substantially unchanged and caused injury, with no proof of carelessness required — and that missing fault element is exactly what separates it from negligence. Restatement section 402A frames the question around a product that is unreasonably dangerous, so a plaintiff who cannot identify any breach of duty still recovers.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-tort exam items give an injured customer and a blameless retailer and ask which theory needs no showing of fault.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: Holds that a firm should satisfy its target market's wants profitably only in ways that also preserve long-run consumer and social welfare — the third test the plain marketing concept leaves out — so an offering that customers genuinely want and the company profits from can still fail this standard because of the harm it does over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions that pit a profitable, popular product against a long-term harm are answered by naming this third test rather than by choosing between customers and profit.

terms.definition: Sets price to earn a stated percentage on invested capital: unit cost + (desired return x invested capital) / expected unit sales. Cost-plus pricing adds a flat markup no matter what the business has invested, so two firms with identical costs but very different capital bases price the same under cost-plus and differently under this method.
terms.whyItMatters: A manufacturer roleplay that names a required 20% return on a $2 million plant is asking for this calculation, and a markup answer will not satisfy the judge.

terms.definition: Applies stated go/no-go criteria to drop weak concepts before money is spent, and guards against two opposite errors -- a drop-error that kills a winner and a go-error that carries a loser into costly development; idea generation, by contrast, deliberately withholds all judgment to maximize the count.
terms.whyItMatters: A brainstorming roleplay is scored badly if you evaluate while generating; competitors must say which stage they are in and which error that stage is trying to avoid.

terms.definition: Marketing through online channels such as social media, email, and search.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital promotion reaches audiences efficiently with measurable results.

terms.definition: A short opening section of a report that distills key findings and recommendations.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward a crisp, decision-ready summary.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: Share of one cohort of leads that becomes a qualified opportunity: opportunities created divided by the leads that entered in that same period, never by every lead sitting in the database. 40 opportunities from 500 new leads is 8 percent; dividing by a 12,000-record database reports 0.3 percent and hides the follow-up problem entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel-math items hand you a month of lead counts and opportunity counts and grade the denominator you pick, and a roleplay on tracking prospecting results expects the rate quoted per period rather than against the whole list.

terms.definition: Copies everything changed since the last full backup, so Friday's run is far larger than Monday's, but a restore needs exactly two pieces — the full backup plus the newest run — against the incremental approach's full backup plus every intervening night in sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-continuity roleplay trades nightly window against recovery speed, and the graded answer is which of these two schemes buys the shorter restore.

terms.definition: A structured visit by managers to the actual place work happens, to observe the process and ask questions rather than to inspect people or correct anyone on the spot — the no-blame, observe-only rule is what keeps workers from staging the process for the visitor.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a manager should diagnose a slow process, the expected answer is direct observation at the work site rather than a report or a meeting, which is what an operations judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Checks whether two separate groups' means differ by more than sampling noise, dividing the gap between the means by the standard error of that gap and comparing the result with alpha; it covers two groups only, because running three pairwise tests at 0.05 pushes the chance of at least one false positive to roughly 14 percent, which is what analysis of variance avoids.
terms.whyItMatters: A test-market readout comparing average spend in the treated city against the control city is this test, and the exam wants the two-group limit named before three cities are compared.

terms.definition: Deci and Ryan's account of motivation as three psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — plus a continuum running from purely external regulation through introjected and identified regulation to fully internalized motivation. Motivation is therefore a location on that continuum rather than an amount, and only the internalized end keeps working once the supervisor stops watching.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why a bonus program stopped producing results, or a roleplay on motivating a team without extra budget, is scored on giving choice, competence feedback and belonging instead of raising the payout.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: Divides the standard deviation of period demand by its mean to grade how forecastable a series is: under about 0.25 a single point forecast is dependable, and above roughly 0.50 the item is erratic enough that the plan must carry a range and a buffer instead of one number.
terms.whyItMatters: Planning questions ask which item deserves a statistical forecast and which needs judgment plus safety stock; the ratio decides it, and the threshold is the part of the item being tested.

terms.definition: Invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the share of those invitations that convert into new users — 5 invites at a 25% conversion rate gives k = 1.25 — where any value above 1.0 compounds into self-sustaining growth and any value below 1.0 produces a decaying series that halts on its own once paid acquisition stops, so the threshold is exactly 1.0 and not merely 'high'.
terms.whyItMatters: A referral-program roleplay is scored on stating the break-even threshold and the two inputs you would change to reach it, not on calling the campaign shareable.

terms.definition: Splits the charge into a fixed access fee plus a per-unit price - a club's annual dues plus a per-round greens fee. Because the entry fee captures buyer surplus up front, the usage charge can sit near variable cost, which a single straight per-unit price could never do without giving up the fixed-fee revenue entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Membership and subscription roleplays ask how to raise revenue without raising the usage price, and splitting the charge in two is the move a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: A finished business good that goes into another product and keeps its own identity there -- a car battery, a tire, a microchip; raw materials are processed until that identity is lost, and maintenance and repair supplies never enter the finished product at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Industrial product questions ask you to classify an input; the identity test decides it, and it also explains why component makers can advertise to the end consumer at all.

terms.definition: A retirement account funded with money already taxed, whose qualified withdrawals — contributions and growth alike — come out tax-free.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a young client in a retirement roleplay usually points here, because decades of growth escape tax when the current bracket is low.

terms.definition: Clicks divided by impressions: 250 clicks on 125,000 impressions is 0.2%, which is an ordinary display result and a poor search result. The denominator is impressions served, not people reached, so the figure falls as frequency rises even when the creative is working.
terms.whyItMatters: Campaign-review roleplays hand over a rate that dropped week over week; the competitor is expected to check whether frequency rose before concluding the creative went stale.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: The emotional and rational reasons a customer makes a purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding motives helps position products around what matters.

terms.definition: The mathematical examination of data to identify patterns, test relationships, and support decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are tested on interpreting findings and drawing evidence-based conclusions.

terms.definition: A solicitation that describes a problem and invites vendors to propose their own solution, approach and price, evaluated on weighted criteria beyond cost — where a request for quotation specifies the exact item and quantity already and asks only for price and delivery, making it a lowest-bidder instrument.
terms.whyItMatters: Bid-process roleplays turn on choosing the right document: asking for solutions when you already know the specification wastes vendor effort, and asking only for price on an undefined need produces incomparable bids.

terms.definition: The percentage of candidates who move from one recruiting stage to the next — 400 applicants producing 80 screens is a 20% yield, and 80 screens producing 20 interviews is 25%. Chained backward, the stage yields tell a recruiter how many applicants the top of the funnel must hold to end with a set number of hires: 5 hires at these rates requires roughly 400 applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: Hiring-plan roleplays ask how many applications a posting must attract for four openings, which is solved by multiplying the stage yields, not by guessing.

terms.definition: Internal-consistency measure of how tightly the several items meant to capture one construct move together, on a 0-to-1 scale where 0.70 is the usual floor for a usable multi-item scale and anything above about 0.95 means the items are near-duplicates padding the questionnaire. A high value says the items agree, never that they measure the right thing.
terms.whyItMatters: Evaluating a draft questionnaire means judging whether the five satisfaction items form one scale worth averaging, and this is the number the evaluation reports.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Personal income for an area minus personal tax payments — the disposable dollars residents can actually spend, not gross earnings. It is the income term inside a buying power index, which weights it against the area's population and retail sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Territory and market-selection items give gross income for two cities and expect the after-tax spendable figure to drive the ranking, because a high-tax market supports less spending than its wage level suggests.

terms.definition: Environmental marketing claims the seller cannot substantiate, policed in the United States by the FTC's Green Guides at 16 CFR Part 260, which treat unqualified general claims such as 'eco-friendly' or 'green' as deceptive because they imply every possible environmental benefit, and require a degradability claim to mean complete breakdown within one year of customary disposal; a truthful narrow claim must therefore be stated narrowly to be lawful.
terms.whyItMatters: Sustainability roleplays that ask you to approve a packaging claim are scored on naming the standard and qualifying the claim, since an unqualified benefit statement is a legal exposure, not just a marketing choice.

terms.definition: The price one division charges another inside the same company, which shifts reported profit between units and, across borders, between tax jurisdictions. Section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code requires it to meet the arm's-length standard - the price unrelated parties would have agreed on - so a firm cannot simply invoice its own subsidiary at cost or at zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business roleplays ask why one division's results look poor while the company's consolidated profit is healthy, and the internal price is the mechanism.

terms.definition: The cap a registered apprenticeship program's standards must state under 29 CFR Part 29 on how many apprentices may work per experienced worker on a job — one to one is the common floor, and a sponsor that exceeds its registered figure risks deregistration of the whole program. It travels with a stepped wage schedule: the apprentice begins near 50% of the journeyworker rate and moves up at fixed hour milestones, so the sponsor's cost per apprentice climbs across the term rather than staying flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how a small contractor can afford to train new workers is answered with the supervision ratio and the stepped percentage, and exam items pair it with registered apprenticeship to test whether the competitor knows the arrangement is federally regulated rather than an informal handshake.

terms.definition: Places a pre-release version with outside customers doing real work in their own conditions, capturing failures no internal lab reproduces; alpha testing comes first and is run in-house by employees, so a beta's whole value is the uncontrolled use an alpha deliberately excludes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a limited launch is scored on why outside users are needed before full production, not merely on saying the product will be tested.

terms.definition: The specific group a promotional message is designed to reach.
terms.whyItMatters: Defining the audience shapes the message, media, and timing.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: Total quota handed out across the sales force divided by the revenue the company actually forecasts. Assigning 1.1 to 1.3 times the target is deliberate over-assignment that absorbs ramping reps, mid-year attrition and under-performers, so the plan still lands if some reps miss — it measures quota against target, where pipeline coverage measures open deals against quota.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay that asks you to set quotas for next year is scored on whether you over-assign on purpose and can say why; the exam pairs this with pipeline coverage to see if you can tell the two ratios apart.

terms.definition: A 99.999% uptime commitment, which permits roughly 5.3 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year; each nine dropped multiplies that allowance by ten, so 99.99% permits about 53 minutes, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, and 99% about 3.65 days — which is why a vendor's extra decimal costs so much.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay compares two hosting quotes whose uptime promises differ by one decimal, and converting each into annual minutes is what makes the price gap defensible.

terms.definition: A pre-authorized response to one identified adverse event, naming its trigger, the responsible owner, and the resources released when it fires; a business continuity plan is broader, covering how the whole operation keeps running through any major disruption.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask you to prepare an event team for a supplier failing the week of the show are scored on the trigger, owner, and resource specifics.

terms.definition: Assigning each item a storage location based on picking velocity, unit weight and case cube, so the fastest-moving lines sit closest to packing at waist height — the objective is minimizing picker travel distance, which is the largest single component of order-fulfillment labor.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about slow order fulfillment expect a layout answer tied to pick frequency, not more staff, and the travel-time argument is what makes it persuasive.

terms.definition: Recruiting through referrals, each respondent naming the next, which is often the only practical route into a rare or hidden population; because no one's chance of being reached is known, no sampling error or margin of error can be computed. Quota sampling shares that defect but at least fills preset subgroup counts, while this design lets one social circle dominate.
terms.whyItMatters: A sampling-plan roleplay about reaching a niche buyer, such as competitive drone racers, needs this design named along with the honest admission that the results cannot be projected.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: Splits a revenue miss into three computed pieces that must add back to the total gap: price variance = (actual price − planned price) × actual units; volume variance = (actual units − planned units) × planned price; mix variance = the shift in each product's share of total units valued at planned prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review items give planned and actual price, units and product split and expect all three figures; answering that sales came in soft without the decomposition is exactly what the rubric withholds credit for.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: A business between producer and customer, such as a retailer, wholesaler, or agent.
terms.whyItMatters: Intermediaries expand reach but add cost and control tradeoffs.

terms.definition: Prices the durable base item low and takes the margin on the required consumables or replacement parts - printers and cartridges, razors and blades, a console and its games. Bundle pricing sells the pieces together in one transaction, whereas here the follow-on purchases are separate, repeated, and where the profit actually lives.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-and-pricing roleplays about equipment with proprietary refills expect the candidate to move the two halves of the line in opposite directions.

terms.definition: The contract section fixing measurable performance targets and the credit owed when they are missed: 99.9% monthly uptime allows roughly 43 minutes of outage in a 30-day month, and each tier missed below that refunds a stated percentage of the month's fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-services roleplays ask what the client is actually promised; converting a percentage into allowed minutes and naming the credit is what makes the promise enforceable.

terms.definition: Completed goal actions divided by the visits or clicks that could have completed them — the denominator is sessions, never impressions — so 40 orders from 2,000 landing-page visits is 2% no matter how many people saw the ad that sent them.
terms.whyItMatters: The single most common analytics error on the marketing exam is dividing sales by impressions; an item that supplies impressions, clicks and orders together is checking which denominator the competitor reaches for.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: Closed-won revenue divided by the number of deals won — $480,000 across 60 wins is $8,000 each. It measures one whole customer agreement, where average order value measures one transaction, so a customer who reorders four times a year raises order count without raising this figure at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking you to justify spending more selling time per account is answered by comparing deal size against cost per sales call, not by citing total revenue.

terms.definition: Lets a jury infer a breach of duty from the accident itself when three conditions hold: the harm is of a kind that ordinarily does not happen without carelessness, the instrument causing it was under the defendant's exclusive control, and the plaintiff did nothing to contribute. It shifts the practical burden of explanation onto the defendant in cases where no direct evidence of the careless act exists.
terms.whyItMatters: Tort items about a light fixture falling on a diner test whether the plaintiff can proceed without ever proving what maintenance was skipped.

terms.definition: A cloud arrangement where the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualization while the customer still patches the operating system and everything stacked above it; platform services shift that operating system and runtime to the provider, and software as a service leaves the customer responsible for nothing but their own data and user settings.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks who is at fault when an unpatched server is breached, and the answer depends entirely on which of these three lines the contract drew.

terms.definition: An INTERNAL request from a department asking purchasing to buy something, carrying no commitment to any outside party; the purchase order that purchasing then issues is the EXTERNAL document, and it is the offer that forms a binding contract when the supplier accepts it.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing-control questions ask which document a department head signs and which one legally obligates the company; treating the internal request as the order is the standard error.

terms.definition: Evidence that a scale is not quietly measuring its neighbour: its correlations with measures of a different construct must be clearly lower than its correlations with other measures of the same construct, which is convergent validity. A satisfaction scale correlating 0.85 with a loyalty scale has failed it and the two are one construct, not two.
terms.whyItMatters: When a tracker reports satisfaction and loyalty as separate drivers and both move identically, this is the check that shows the study is double-counting one thing.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: Isolates the profit effect of selling a different blend than planned: for each item, (its actual share of total units − its planned share) × total actual units × that item's planned contribution per unit, summed across the line — so a firm can hit its unit target exactly and still miss profit by shifting volume onto the thinner-margin product.
terms.whyItMatters: Shortfall questions where total units met plan are solved with this term alone, and it is the numeric case for paying sales incentives on contribution rather than on units sold.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of how threatened a culture feels by ambiguity, which predicts how much written structure a message must carry: high scorers such as Greece near 100 and Japan near 92 expect detailed agendas, explicit rules and signed detail before acting, while low scorers such as Singapore near 8 and Denmark near 23 will work from an open-ended proposal. It is not risk aversion in the financial sense - a high-scoring culture may take a very large risk, provided the procedure for taking it is spelled out.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to prepare for a first meeting with a Japanese partner is scored on sending the agenda and documentation in advance rather than planning to improvise.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.definition: An agreement among competitors to set, raise, peg or stabilize what they charge - including agreeing on discounts, credit terms or a shared formula rather than on a final number. Section 1 of the Sherman Act treats it as per se illegal, so no business justification is a defense, unlike conscious parallelism, where rivals simply match a published price with no agreement and commit no offense.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics-in-pricing items describe two owners comparing rates at a trade show, and the tested point is that the agreement itself, not any proven harm, is the violation.

terms.definition: Scores quality as perception minus expectation on paired 22-item scales across five dimensions -- reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness -- so a dimension scoring 0 means expectations were met exactly and every negative number is a measured shortfall to fix.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how you would measure service quality is scored on the subtraction: measuring satisfaction alone cannot tell an over-promise from an under-delivery.

terms.definition: Government and industry rules governing ad claims, content, and disclosure.
terms.whyItMatters: Compliance protects consumers and shields a business from liability.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: Damping an emotion after it has already arrived by hiding its outward signs, rather than changing the interpretation that produced it. Because it is applied late, it leaves the physiological arousal fully intact, raises blood pressure in the person watching as well, and measurably impairs memory for what was said during the episode -- the opposite profile from cognitive reappraisal, which is applied early and carries none of those costs.
terms.whyItMatters: When a Human Resources Management Series judge asks how you would hold composure while an employee vents about a denied raise, an answer built on hiding what you felt names the strategy research links to worse recall of the conversation; the scoring answer reinterprets the outburst before it peaks.

terms.definition: Every open deal multiplied by the win probability its current stage carries, then summed. A $200,000 deal sitting in a 30 percent stage counts as $60,000, so $1.4 million of raw pipeline spread across early stages may weight to under $400,000 — the total becomes a forecast instead of a list of what is theoretically in play.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting items give a table of deal values and stage probabilities and expect the weighted total, not the sum; in a roleplay defending a forecast to a manager, quoting raw pipeline reads as the rookie answer.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: A supplier-provided document in a fixed sixteen-section order under the Globally Harmonized System, covering hazards, handling, exposure controls, first aid and disposal — the fixed section order is the point, because a responder finds first-aid information in the same place on every sheet.
terms.whyItMatters: A chemical-spill roleplay expects you to say where the handling and first-aid instructions live and that the sheets must be accessible to employees on the shift, not filed in a manager's office.

terms.definition: Ordered measurement with equal gaps between adjacent points but no true zero, so differences can be added and averaged while ratios cannot: 40 degrees is not twice as warm as 20, and a 7-point agreement rating of 6 is not twice the agreement of 3. A ratio scale such as dollars spent or units sold has the true zero and does permit the ratio.
terms.whyItMatters: Deciding whether a questionnaire's answers may be averaged, or only counted, turns on which level of measurement each question produced.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Annual dividends per share divided by share price, stating income return as a percentage so a dividend stock can be compared against a savings rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking for income rather than growth in a retirement roleplay is asking about this figure, which moves whenever the share price moves.

terms.definition: The average signed error across periods — actual minus forecast with the plus and minus signs kept — so persistent over-forecasting shows up as a running negative. It measures direction, where MAPE measures size, and a plan can post a respectable MAPE while drifting the same way every single month.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-review items give a run of months that miss high every time and ask what is wrong with the method; the answer is a systematic error in the assumptions, not random noise.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: Cutting price below an appropriate measure of cost - courts generally use average variable cost - to drive rivals out, with a realistic prospect of recouping the losses later through higher prices. The Brooke Group standard requires both elements, which is what separates it from a loss leader, where a below-cost item exists only to pull traffic for other purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-considerations questions turn on the recoupment element, so a candidate who simply says selling below cost is illegal is scored wrong.

terms.definition: Sells the finished product with its full marketing plan in a few representative cities while matched control cities keep the old plan, so the result read is the difference between the two areas rather than the test area's raw sales; the cost is secrecy, since rivals see the plan months early.
terms.whyItMatters: Launch roleplays ask how you would prove the plan works before national rollout; the matched control is the detail that turns a demo into a measurement.

terms.definition: A purchase credited to an ad that was served and seen but never clicked, counted only when it falls inside a fixed look-back window — commonly one day for display against 30 days for a click — which is why these totals overstate a campaign next to click-through conversions.
terms.whyItMatters: A results presentation where the platform's reported sales exceed the client's actual order count is this in action, and the competitor is expected to say which conversions were assumed rather than observed.

terms.definition: A systematic study of a job's duties, responsibilities, and required skills.
terms.whyItMatters: It informs hiring standards and identifies the right competencies for a role.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: Purchase price plus installation, training, consumables, maintenance and downtime across the asset's life, minus its resale value — so a $12,000 machine burning $400 of supplies a year beats a $9,000 machine burning $1,600 within five years. It answers a price objection by moving the comparison from acquisition price to lifetime cost.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer says a competitor quoted less, judges look for this calculation rather than a discount, because conceding on price is the response the rubric marks down.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: An arrangement where the supplier monitors the buyer's usage data and decides replenishment timing and quantity, while the buyer still owns and pays for the stock on hand — consignment differs precisely there: the supplier retains ownership until the item is sold or consumed.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays ask who should hold the replenishment decision and who carries the cash tied up in the stock; the ownership line is what separates the two arrangements.
