terms.definition: Percent of respondents picking either of the two most favorable options on a rating scale, the 4s and 5s on a five-point scale, reported instead of the average because averages hide splits: ratings of 1, 1, 5, 5 and ratings of 3, 3, 3, 3 both average 3.0, yet the first scores 50 percent here and the second scores zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Reporting satisfaction tracking to a manager means choosing between the mean and this share, and a polarized customer base is only visible in the second.

terms.term: Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act
terms.definition: Federal statute obliging an employer of 100 or more employees to give 60 calendar days' written notice before a plant closing that ends 50 or more jobs at one site within any 30-day window, or a mass layoff of 500 workers — or of 50 to 499 when that reaches a third of the site's active workforce. Skipping notice is not a fine paid to the government: the remedy is back pay and benefits owed to each affected worker for every day of shortfall, capped at 60.
terms.whyItMatters: Worker-rights exam items use the 60-day count to kill distractors, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays an employee hearing closing rumors is scored on stating the notice entitlement and the back-pay remedy instead of offering reassurance.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: The percentage change in unit sales delivered by a one-percent change in advertising spending — 3% more volume on 10% more spend is 0.3 — and because measured values usually sit near 0.1 to 0.2, doubling the budget rarely comes close to doubling volume; compare it against price elasticity before choosing which lever to pull.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget-allocation items supply both elasticities and expect the higher-return lever chosen with the arithmetic shown; a plan that asks for more advertising without this number has no answer when the judge asks why not a price move instead.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.

terms.definition: Restricts a category to a few preset price points - say $29, $59 and $99 - and buys merchandise to fit them rather than pricing each item off its own cost. Psychological tactics change the digits shown at a single price point, whereas this decides how many price points the assortment offers at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Apparel-buying roleplays ask how a store can carry forty styles without paralyzing shoppers, and the answer is the number of price points rather than the number of items.

terms.definition: Locates a failure in one of five gaps -- not knowing what customers expect, setting wrong standards, delivery that misses those standards, promotion promising what operations cannot deliver, and the customer gap between expectation and perception, which is produced by the first four.
terms.whyItMatters: Guest-recovery roleplays are scored on diagnosing which gap caused the complaint, since an over-promising ad and an untrained server call for opposite fixes.

terms.definition: A sourcing decision comparing the relevant in-house cost — incremental variable cost plus any avoidable fixed cost — against the supplier's price plus transaction and quality-control cost; unavoidable fixed overhead is excluded from the in-house side because it continues either way.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply a per-unit production cost, a quoted supplier price, and an allocated overhead line, and the tested trap is including the overhead that does not disappear.

terms.definition: A schedule that alternates concentrated bursts with hiatus periods carrying no advertising at all — eight weeks on, four weeks dark — which buys higher in-season frequency than a flat continuous weight, at the cost of awareness decay during the dark weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Seasonal-business roleplays turn on choosing this over pulsing or continuity, and the competitor is expected to name the trade the client is making rather than simply calling the plan seasonal.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: Ramped headcount times individual quota times the attainment rate the team really achieves — 20 reps carrying $500,000 each but hitting 70 percent supports $7 million of revenue, not the $10 million the quota sheet implies. Skipping the attainment factor is what makes a hiring plan promise revenue the team has never once delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: A growth-planning roleplay that asks how many reps to hire to reach a revenue goal is graded on multiplying in historical attainment; the exam tests it as a three-factor calculation.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: Recordable injuries and illnesses multiplied by 200,000, divided by total hours worked — the 200,000 representing 100 full-time employees working a 2,000-hour year, which is what makes a small firm's figure comparable with a large one's.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety roleplays give an injury count and an hours-worked total and ask whether the site is above its industry benchmark; a raw injury count cannot be benchmarked and is scored as an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Selling across store, web, app and marketplace on ONE shared inventory pool, price and customer record, so a shopper can start a purchase in one place and finish it in another. The test that separates it from multichannel is integration: multichannel runs each channel as a separate P&L with its own stock and pricing, so an order begun online cannot be returned or completed in the store.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and marketing roleplays ask you to fix a customer who bought online and was refused a store return — the answer names the missing integration, not better staff training.

terms.definition: Multiplies the standard error by the square root of (N minus n) divided by (N minus 1), shrinking it when the sample is a large slice of a small population; it is ignored until the sample passes roughly 5 percent of the population, which is why 400 respondents buy nearly the same precision in a town of 8,000 as in a nation of 300 million.
terms.whyItMatters: It settles the recurring roleplay objection that a national sample of 1,000 must be too small, because precision tracks the sample size rather than the fraction of the population covered.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: Carries advertising effect forward as this week's effect = this week's spending effect + (retention rate × last week's carried effect); at a retention rate of 0.7 a flight that ends today still delivers 70% of its pull next week and 49% the week after, which is why a brand can stop spending and not lose sales immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-scheduling questions ask whether a brand can go dark for a month, and this decay arithmetic answers it; it also fixes how long after a campaign ends a plan may still credit sales to that campaign.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: A supplier's agreement with its dealers fixing the minimum price they may resell at. The Leegin decision moved minimum RPM from per se illegal to a rule-of-reason analysis under federal law, though several states still bar it outright; a minimum advertised price policy differs because it restricts only the advertised figure and leaves the checkout price free.
terms.whyItMatters: Manufacturer-channel roleplays ask whether a brand may stop a discounter from undercutting its dealers, and the answer depends on this distinction.

terms.definition: Cuts a plaintiff's award by the share of fault assigned to them — a pure system pays even a plaintiff who is 90% at fault, while a modified system bars recovery once fault reaches 50% or 51%. The older contributory-negligence rule, still law in a few states, denies any recovery at all to a plaintiff who is even 1% at fault, and that all-or-nothing contrast is what exam items are actually testing.
terms.whyItMatters: A slip-and-fall damages question gives $100,000 in harm and 30% plaintiff fault and asks what the business actually pays.

terms.definition: Something buyers do not think to look for and may not know exists, so it has to be sold to them rather than bought -- burial plots, life insurance, a brand-new category's first entrant; a specialty good is the opposite pole, actively hunted by name with special effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling roleplays for insurance or services are scored on recognizing that no one walks in asking, which forces prospecting and personal selling rather than displays.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: Diagnosing the buyer's problem through questioning and recommending the right fit even when that means a smaller order, as against transactional selling, which moves a known item at speed and treats the exchange as complete at the register. The dividing line is who defines the need: the buyer arrives with it in a transaction, the rep uncovers it here.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer asks for a product that will not solve their stated problem, the rubric credits the competitor who redirects the recommendation over the one who rings up the request.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: Sorts national communication styles into three categories rather than scoring dimensions: linear-active cultures (Germany, Switzerland, the U.S.) plan sequentially, do one thing at a time and argue from facts; multi-active cultures (Italy, Brazil, much of Africa) speak over one another, run several tasks at once and put the relationship ahead of the schedule; reactive cultures (Japan, China, Finland) listen first, do not interrupt, and answer only after a silence that outsiders misread as disagreement. Each country lands in one category, which is what makes it usable mid-meeting where a six-dimension score is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay in which the counterpart falls silent after your proposal is scored on reading the pause as a reactive-style norm instead of filling it with an unnecessary concession.

terms.definition: A formal document requesting goods or services from a vendor at set terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchase orders create the paper trail for efficient procurement.

terms.definition: Weighted composite of a market area's share of national income, retail sales and population, conventionally 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, summing to that area's percent of national buying power: 2 percent of income, 3 percent of retail sales and 4 percent of population gives 1.0 plus 0.9 plus 0.8, or 2.7 percent. Population alone overstates a poor, crowded market.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing which metro gets the next store or the next media flight is decided on this weighted share rather than headcount, and the weights are the part competitors forget.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: Takes last period's actual as next period's number and nothing else, and exists to be the benchmark: compute its error first, and any model whose MAPE is not meaningfully below that baseline is not paying for the effort it costs, however advanced the technique behind it sounds.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which forecasting approach a firm should keep; the defensible answer is whichever one beats the zero-effort baseline by a measured margin, and a plan that cannot show that improvement loses the argument for its forecasting spend.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: A rise in performance produced by a supervisor's high expectations, transmitted through the extra coaching, harder assignments, longer response time and warmer feedback those expectations quietly cause — Rosenthal's finding that the expectation, not the measured ability, moved the outcome. Its negative twin, the Golem effect, does identical damage in the downward direction.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why two equally skilled new hires diverge under different supervisors expects this, and coaching roleplays are graded on assigning stretch work to the employee the manager privately doubts.

terms.definition: The buyer's tendency to judge a price against the first figure they encounter, so a $199 compare-at number makes $149 read as a bargain. Marketers separate the internal reference price a shopper carries in memory from the external one printed on the tag, and the FTC requires that any advertised former price actually have been charged.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-pricing roleplays ask a candidate to defend a compare-at price to a judge, which needs both the psychology and the former-price disclosure rule.

terms.definition: The band between desired service, what the customer hopes for, and adequate service, the least they will accept: performance inside the band passes unnoticed, above it delights, below it triggers complaint or defection, and the band narrows sharply in urgent or first-time-fix situations.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about exceeding guest expectations are scored on knowing that ordinary delivery earns nothing; the band explains why effort spent in the middle is invisible.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: Count of deals where the buyer bought nothing at all, divided by all closed-lost deals — not by all opportunities. If 60 of 100 losses were no-decisions, the problem is urgency and the business case, because a buyer who chose a rival was at least persuaded to purchase; splitting losses this way points at two completely different fixes.
terms.whyItMatters: A win-loss review roleplay is scored on separating the two loss types before recommending anything, and the exam plants a competitor-versus-status-quo distinction in the stem.

terms.definition: The sum of a project's future cash flows discounted back to today's dollars, minus its initial cost — positive means the project earns more than the required return.
terms.whyItMatters: Capital-investment items ask whether to buy the equipment, and the sign of this figure is the answer regardless of how large the raw cash flows look.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: How many times inventory is sold and replaced over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Turnover reveals inventory efficiency and its impact on cash flow.

terms.definition: A brand's advertising spend divided by total category advertising spend over the same period, so $2 million inside a $20 million category is 10 percent. Held against market share it becomes a plan: a brand whose voice share exceeds its market share is buying growth, and one whose voice share sits below it is harvesting a position it is no longer defending.
terms.whyItMatters: Tracking a campaign against competitors requires a spend-relative measure, since raw dollars up 10 percent still lose ground when the category's spend is up 30 percent.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: The number of weeks it takes a campaign's carried-over effect to fall to 50% of its starting level, computed from the weekly retention rate as ln(0.5) ÷ ln(rate) — a rate of 0.7 gives about 1.9 weeks — so a short half-life forces flights roughly monthly while a long one permits long gaps between bursts.
terms.whyItMatters: Flighting-versus-continuity items expect the weeks figure computed, not a description of the trade-off, and the same number sets the measurement window a plan claims when it attributes sales to a campaign.

terms.definition: Number hired divided by number of applicants — 8 hires from 400 applicants is 0.02. Unlike a yield ratio, which measures one stage, this compares the two ends of the funnel, and a smaller number means a more selective process: 0.02 gives the employer far more room to be choosy than 0.50 does.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing questions pair the selection ratio with a test's validity to argue that a screening tool only adds value when the employer has many applicants per opening.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: A supplier rule conditioning co-op advertising support on retailers not promoting below a stated figure, while leaving the actual transaction price untouched. Announced unilaterally under the Colgate doctrine it involves no agreement at all, which is why it carries less antitrust exposure than resale price maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-conflict roleplays about a retailer's online listing are resolved by knowing that what is controlled is the advertised number, not the price the customer pays at checkout.

terms.definition: A tangible item expected to survive repeated use, the standard statistical cutoff being an expected life of three years or more, which is why appliances and vehicles qualify; nondurables are consumed in one or a few uses and are bought on habit rather than deliberation.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty, financing, and personal-selling effort all follow this split, so an exam item on why one product gets a service plan and another does not is answered with the three-year line.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: An employer rule capping what any manager may tell a reference checker — dates of employment, job title, and sometimes final pay — adopted because a former employer's comment on performance holds its qualified privilege only while made in good faith and loses it, opening a defamation claim, once malice or reckless falsehood is shown. It is not a universal shield: a handful of states run service-letter statutes, Missouri's being the model, that compel a letter stating the cause of separation within 45 days of a certified-mail request from anyone who worked at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: Professional-development roleplays hand the competitor a manager who wants to warn another firm about a fired employee, and the graded answer is the disclosure limit plus the legal reason for it; job-search exam items use the same rule to explain why a former supervisor will confirm only dates.

terms.definition: A short-window, fixed-dollar bonus paid per unit on one targeted product — $50 a unit for 30 days, frequently funded by the manufacturer and paid outside the regular commission plan. An accelerator instead lifts the commission percentage on everything sold past quota, so one steers which item gets pushed and the other rewards total volume.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selling items describe a vendor paying a retailer's floor staff per unit and ask what the payment is; a promotion roleplay expects you to name the mechanism that redirects selling effort to one slow-moving SKU.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Inspecting products and services to ensure they meet set standards.
terms.whyItMatters: It catches defects early, protecting satisfaction and reducing waste.

terms.definition: Estimates market potential by starting from a broad population count and multiplying through a chain of narrowing percentages: 2,000,000 residents times 40 percent in the target age times 30 percent who own a pet times 25 percent who buy premium food times $200 spent a year yields $12,000,000. Every shaky percentage in the chain compounds into the final number.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship or research roleplay that asks how big the opportunity is wants this chain shown step by step, with the source of each percentage named.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: A firm's obligations beyond profit, organized in Carroll's pyramid as economic, then legal, then ethical, then philanthropic layers, where the lower layers are required and the top layer is desired; the ordering is what stops it from being read as charity alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics exam items ask which layer a described action occupies, and community donations by a firm that is violating labor law is the classic mis-ordering trap.

terms.definition: The distance between the top-down number corporate assumes and the sum of the territory-level bottom-up forecasts, stated as a percentage of the top-down total; a gap past roughly 5% has to be closed by named actions with volume attached to each before the plan is approved, never by splitting the difference.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-approval scenarios hand a corporate target and the field's rolled-up total and expect the gap quantified and assigned; the judge's follow-up is always which specific actions close it and what each is worth.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: The 1936 amendment to the Clayton Act barring a seller from charging competing buyers different prices for commodities of like grade and quality where competition may be injured. Two defenses exist - cost justification and meeting a competitor's price in good faith - and because it reaches goods rather than services, a service firm's tiered rates fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Wholesale roleplays ask whether a special volume deal for one chain is lawful, and the expected answer names the cost-justification defense rather than the size of the discount.

terms.definition: The severest federal recall classification, used when a defect carries a reasonable probability of serious injury or death; Class II covers defects whose harm is temporary or medically reversible and where serious harm is remote, and Class III covers violations unlikely to cause any harm.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-protection questions give a defect scenario and ask how urgently the firm must act; the class decides the notification reach and the speed regulators expect.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: An intermediary that buys goods in bulk from producers and resells them to retailers.
terms.whyItMatters: Wholesalers aggregate inventory and provide the logistics that enable retail networks.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: Quantifying the buyer's gain in the buyer's own numbers — hours saved times loaded labor rate, or scrap avoided times unit cost — so the proposal shows a payback period instead of a feature list. Feature-benefit selling states what a feature does for the customer; this states what that outcome is worth in dollars per year.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business roleplays that give you the client's volumes and costs are asking for a dollar case, and a competitor who only lists benefits leaves the quantified point unscored.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: The square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order) divided by annual holding cost per unit — the single order size where rising carrying cost and falling ordering cost cross and total cost bottoms out.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay that asks you to cut the cost of holding stock is answered with this trade-off, not with 'order less': you must say that ordering more often lowers carrying cost but raises order cost, and name the quantity where the two balance.

terms.definition: Share of a page's total views that were the last page of the session, exits divided by that page's pageviews, which is not the bounce rate: bounces count only sessions that both began and ended on that page, divided by sessions that began there. An order-confirmation page should show a high exit rate and a near-zero bounce rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Diagnosing where a checkout funnel leaks means telling a page people leave from after doing something from a page people never engage with at all, and the two metrics disagree constantly.

terms.definition: A business owned and run by two or more people who share profits and liabilities.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership law sets how partners share profits, decide, and bear business debts.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: The spending level on a diminishing-returns response curve where the last dollar invested returns exactly one dollar of contribution; below it more spending still adds profit, above it volume keeps climbing while profit falls, so the stopping test is marginal contribution per marginal dollar equal to 1.0 — not whether total return is still positive.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget items deliberately show total return positive at every spending level to see whether the competitor stops at the marginal break-even; a plan arguing for more spend past that point is refuted with its own numbers.

terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: Rewards total volume purchased across a stated period, so a buyer's separate orders add together toward the break. A noncumulative discount resets with every order, which is why the cumulative form builds account loyalty while the noncumulative one is far easier to defend as cost-justified under Robinson-Patman.
terms.whyItMatters: Distributor roleplays ask which discount structure stops an account from splitting its orders among three suppliers, and the two forms give opposite answers.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: The point inside a speaker's turn - a completed clause, a finished idea, a falling intonation - at which someone else may take the floor without it counting as an interruption. Conversation analysis clocks the median gap between turns at about 200 milliseconds across languages, so speech beginning before one of these points is an interruption while speech beginning at one is a harmless overlap, and a silence stretched past roughly 700 milliseconds is itself heard as reluctance or disagreement.
terms.whyItMatters: Group-discussion and team-event judges score whether a competitor gets into the conversation without cutting anyone off, which is a finer rule than 'wait until they stop talking.'

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: The FTC rule confining outbound sales calls to a residence to the hours between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. in the customer's local time zone, and requiring the caller to state who is calling, what is being sold and the total cost before taking any payment. A New York center dialing California at 8:30 p.m. Eastern is legal because the customer's clock reads 5:30 p.m.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items plant a two-time-zone call and ask whether it is lawful, which is decided by the customer's local hour; an outbound-calling roleplay expects the disclosure sequence before any card number is requested.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: Planning, executing, and monitoring work to hit objectives within time and budget.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets managers coordinate resources and deliver on schedule.

terms.definition: Catching and sharing another person's feeling state directly instead of inferring it from the outside. It is the branch that reliably triggers helping in the moment, and also the branch that exhausts the helper: compassion fatigue in caregiving and front-line service tracks affective empathy, not the cognitive kind, which is why high-empathy staff burn out faster than indifferent ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and Human Resources roleplays that ask you to coach a front-desk team through a month of hostile guests are scored on whether your plan protects the staff who feel the most, and naming which branch of empathy causes the burnout is what separates a top answer from a sympathetic one.

terms.definition: Assigns 100 percent of a conversion's credit to the final channel the buyer used before purchase, which reliably overpays branded search and retargeting and starves the awareness channels a first-touch model would credit instead; a linear model splits the credit evenly across every touch, and the three models can rank the same channels in opposite orders.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending where next quarter's budget goes is a trap when the report behind it uses one attribution rule, so the model has to be named before the ranking is trusted.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: The percentage volume increase a discount must produce merely to hold contribution flat: discount per unit ÷ (normal contribution per unit − discount per unit). A $1 cut against $4 of unit contribution needs 33% more units; a $2 cut against the same $4 needs 100%, which is why deep cuts almost never pay for themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-approval questions give margin and discount depth and expect the required lift computed and compared with the forecast lift; anything forecast below the break-even figure is a promotion the plan should reject.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: State laws capping increases on essentials once a disaster or emergency is formally declared, many of them fixing a numeric trigger such as more than 10% above the pre-emergency price or above the seller's own documented cost increase. There is no federal counterpart, so legality depends on the state and on the declaration being in force.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics question about raising generator prices during a hurricane tests whether the competitor knows the trigger is the declared emergency, not merely a high price.

terms.definition: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price, which buys more shares when prices are low and lowers the average cost per share over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment roleplays ask how a client should handle a volatile market, and this is the answer that beats trying to time an entry point.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.
